solutions.latex:
Let $u = 3x^3$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 9x^2$. By the chain rule,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos 3x^3 &= -\sin(3x^3)\cdot 9x^2 \\ &= -9x^2\sin 3x^3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the derivative of the function $y=\tan(x^2)$.
By using an appropriate trigonometric identity, find $\displaystyle\int x\tan^2(x^2)\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the Pythagorean identity $\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int x\tan^2(x^2)\,dx&=\int x\left(\sec^2(x^2)-1\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x\left(\sec^2(x^2)-1\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int\left(2x\sec^2(x^2)-2x\right)dx\\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\tan(x^2)-x^2\right)+C &&(\text{using part (a)}) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expresses integrand with appropriate Pythagorean identity, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{3}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the reference sheet:
$$\int f'(x)\sec^2f(x)\,dx=\tan f(x)+c$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{1}{3}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)dx&=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_{\frac{1}{3}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\dfrac{\pi}{2}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)dx\\&=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)\right]_{\frac{1}{3}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]\\&=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\left[1-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right]\\&=\dfrac{6-2\sqrt{3}}{3\pi}\\&=\dfrac{2(3-\sqrt{3})}{3\pi}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive $\dfrac{2}{\pi}\left[\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)\right]$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which of the following is an expression for $\displaystyle\int\left(\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}+\dfrac{1}{1-\sin x}\right)dx$?

solutions.latex:
Use the identity $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\tan^2x\,dx &= \int(\sec^2x-1)\,dx \\ &= \tan x-x+c \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: What values of $k$ result in $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin(kx)\,dx=0$, where $k$ is an integer?

solutions.latex:
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$$
\exfigure{161_q8_s1}
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^{\pi}\sin(kx)\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{\cos(kx)}{k}\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= \dfrac{1-\cos(k\pi)}{k} \end{aligned}$$
This is $0$ only when $\cos(k\pi)=1$, that is, when $k$ is even (the interval $[0,\pi]$ then holds a whole number of periods); for odd $k$ it is $\dfrac{2}{k}\ne0$.

parts.latex: Which of the following functions is a primitive of $x+\cos x$ ?

solutions.latex:
A primitive is an antiderivative, so integrate term by term.
$$\int (x+\cos x)\,dx=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\sin x+C$$
Check by differentiating option D: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\sin x\right)=x+\cos x$. Options A and B differentiate to $\cos x$ and $-\cos x$, and C gives $x-\cos x$.

parts.latex:
The graph of the primitive function of $f(x)=\tan^2x$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Find the primitive function, leaving all values in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Use the identity $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int\tan^2x\,dx \\ &= \int\left(\sec^2x-1\right)dx \\ &= \tan x-x+C \end{aligned}$$
The graph crosses the $x$-axis at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}+C \\ 0 &= \sqrt{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{3}+C \\ C &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\tan x-x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}$$
criteria: Finds $F(x)=\tan x-x+C$ and substitutes $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx$ Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Expands and uses the identity, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2\right)=2x$, write the integrand as $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2x\sin x^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^2 2x\sin x^2\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos x^2\right]_0^2 \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 4-1) \\ &\approx 0.83 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int_0^2 x\sin x^2\,dx\approx 0.83$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Multiply the numerator and denominator by $e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{e^x}{e^{-x}-e^x}\,dx &= \int\dfrac{e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}}\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{-2e^{2x}}{1-e^{2x}}\,dx \\ &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|1-e^{2x}\right|+C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int\dfrac{e^x}{e^{-x}-e^x}\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|1-e^{2x}\right|+C$$
